Dúnedain of the Lost Realm

The Dúnedain of Arnor descend from the Faithful who followed Elendil north after the Downfall of Númenor. Their kinsmen founded Gondor in the south; they established the Northern Realm in Exile in Eriador. Dynastic division, wars against Angmar, and the gradual abandonment of its cities later undid that power. The descendants of the survivors preserve the memory of institutions and estates that have sometimes left few visible traces.

Lineages of Arnor

This Culture embraces the old Dúnedain lineages of Arnor, Arthedain, Cardolan, and Rhudaur, along with their descendants after the Northern Kingdom vanished. It may represent a noble or officer of the former courts, but equally a Ranger, keeper of an isolated estate, leader of a small community, or guardian of Eriador's roads.

Their upbringing preserves the learning of a once highly organised society. From childhood, they are taught languages, history, arms, leadership, and the duties attached to their birth. Their military traditions give them access to every kind of armour and many weapons, while clothing, equipment, and family possessions still bear witness to fine craftsmanship.

The Northern Kingdom

At its height, Arnor stretched across much of Eriador. Its roads linked Annúminas, Fornost, Amon Sûl, and the western lands, while forts and watchtowers guarded the approaches. The Northern Dúnedain remember this network even where grass has swallowed the old roads.

Heritages of Arthedain, Cardolan, and Rhudaur

Arthedain preserved the royal line and Elendil's customs the longest. Cardolan suffered more heavily from war, migration, and the gradual disappearance of its great houses; conflict and foreign influence altered Rhudaur's inheritance more profoundly. These different histories still shape the traditions of their descendants.

After the fall of Fornost

The fall of Fornost ended the kingdom's political power. Those who survived withdrew to hidden refuges and continued their duty without the courts, garrisons, or resources that had once supported Arnor. Protecting roads and settlements became the work of families and small bands.

Appearance and longevity

The Dúnedain of Arnor are tall and strongly built, with a noble bearing. Like their kin in Gondor, they generally have fair skin, black or dark-brown hair, and grey, blue, green, or hazel eyes. Those whose lineages retain the strongest Númenórean ancestry often have little or no beard.

Their maximum lifespan generally ranges from 160 to 200 years, somewhat below that of Gondor’s highest lineages. In families that have intermarried with the peoples of Eriador, it may instead fall between 90 and 125 years. Their constitution and resistance to disease may then more closely resemble those of Common Men.

These differences between lineages are especially apparent in the former lands of Cardolan and Rhudaur. Two characters who claim Dúnadan descent may share stories, customs, and obligations while differing considerably in ancestry and lifespan.

Arnorian society

Under its kings, Arnor was home to a learned and hierarchical society. Noble houses maintained genealogies, governed fortified estates, and educated their heirs in languages, diplomacy, law, and arms. Many customs reached back to Númenor and were preserved in writing as well as speech.

Life among the survivors

The disasters of the North later imposed a more austere existence. Descendants of the old houses learned to live with little, protect villages whose inhabitants sometimes knew nothing of their origins, and lead by example rather than the outward signs of rank.

Their reserve reflects their upbringing, inherited responsibilities, and the need to travel unnoticed. They seldom discuss their ancestry with strangers and often pass as hunters, soldiers, or ordinary travellers.

Memory and duty

Arnor's ruins belong to their everyday landscape. Unlike their kinsmen in Gondor, who still inhabit thriving cities, the Northern Dúnedain travel abandoned roads, pass fallen towers and burial mounds, and cross deserted estates; some strongholds have even fallen into enemy hands.

The experience of loss brings melancholy, but also stubborn patience. They know a task may outlast several generations and that victory is never assured. Their understanding of duty rests on endurance, secrecy, and a willingness to make necessary sacrifices.

The threat of Angmar

The threat from the North remains vivid in their memory: Angmar, Orcs, corrupted Men, and the creatures roaming the old royal lands. The Witch-king's disappearance has not ended their vigilance for signs of his former power.

Travel and self-reliance

Before the kingdom's ruin, the Dúnedain lived in towns, lordly estates, and fortresses. Many later dispersed among hidden refuges, protected villages, and remote holdings, sometimes leading semi-nomadic lives. Some continued to farm; others became hunters, messengers, scouts, or guardians.

Such a life demands self-reliance. Travelling unnoticed, following tracks, finding old roads, surviving in woods or on moors, repairing equipment, and treating common injuries are skills taught to young Dúnedain.

The self-reliance acquired on the roads and in hidden refuges complements their older education. Many can still read northern chronicles, speak several languages, and explain the customs of Arnorian institutions that vanished long ago.

Faith and remembrance of the dead

Their faith is quietly observed. They revere Eru and the Valar without a powerful priesthood or frequent public ceremonies. Speaking truthfully, keeping one's word, honouring the dead, and carrying out one's duty are tangible ways of remaining faithful to this inheritance.

Tombs, barrows, and memorials of former kings are treated with care. Where a villager sees a collapsed wall, a Dúnadan may recognise the estate of an allied house or the grave of a captain forgotten elsewhere. Stories and genealogies thus give meaning to the places they travel through.

The Northern Dúnedain share their Gondorian kinsmen's fear of death. War and Arnor's ruin have nevertheless taught them a measure of acceptance: their chief concern is to fulfil a duty that their descendants can carry on.

Languages

Westron serves everyday needs; Adûnaic remains the language of ancestors and scholarship. Sindarin matters in noble houses, relations with Rivendell, and the handing down of history. Quenya belongs chiefly to ancient writings, ceremonies, and learned study.

Depending on region and period, they may also know Dunael, Blarm, Eriadorian dialects, the languages of the Northmen, and certain forms of communication used by scouts and guardians.

Dress and family heirlooms

Old court dress combined linen, silk, wool, embroidery, wide sleeves, worked belts, and fur cloaks. Arnor's survivors adapted these traditions to travel: subdued colours, sturdy boots, heavy cloaks, and reinforced garments. Jewellery, embroidery, and family emblems are often kept out of sight.

Their most treasured possessions pass from one generation to the next: a sword, brooch, ring, scabbard, fragment of a banner, or the seal of a vanished house. Their worth often lies less in the material than in the names, memories, and oaths associated with them.

Weapons and equipment

The Dúnedain of Arnor have access to every kind of armor and possess the constitution required to wear the heaviest. Their traditional arsenal includes broadswords, longswords, or bastard swords, battle axes, spears, long and composite bows, halberds, maces, flails, warhammers, two-handed weapons, and war mattocks.

After the kingdom's loss, the Dúnedain favour weapons and armour suited to travel: sword, bow, short spear, light shield, mail, and a travelling cloak. Such equipment serves patrols, reconnaissance, ambushes, and the defence of travellers and threatened passes.

Training

Their education covers diplomacy, history, leadership, medicine, music, languages, runes, riding, tactics, tracking, navigation, and many military or craft arts.

Dúnedain of Arnor characters

This Culture suits descendants of Arthedain's houses, surviving families of Cardolan, Dúnedain of the Angle, loyal heirs of Rhudaur's nobility, and the Rangers of the North. It may also represent those who watch over a hidden refuge, a forgotten estate, or the heirs of Isildur.

The Dúnedain of Arnor guard the memory of a vanished kingdom. Oath and duty bind them more closely than the lands they still rule. Among the ruins of the North, they preserve a distant hope of restoration and quietly protect communities that often remain unaware of their presence.
